lesson.title: Which Way Is It Going? Direction from the Sign of Velocity
lesson.summary: The sign of v(t) tells you an object's direction of motion along its path: positive means moving one way, negative means moving the other way, and zero means momentarily at rest, though not always a reversal.
lesson.body:
Since velocity is signed, as the last chapter established, that sign is not just leftover bookkeeping, it directly answers which way this object is moving right now. Reading direction from velocity is one of the most immediately useful things a derivative can tell you about motion.

If v(t) > 0, the object is moving in the positive direction (however positive is defined for the setup, often right or up). If v(t) < 0, it's moving in the negative direction (left or down). If v(t) = 0, the object is momentarily at rest at that instant; this may or may not be a moment of reversal, a point worth checking carefully rather than assuming.

Using v(t) = 3(t - 1)(t - 3) from s(t) = t^3 - 6t^2 + 9t, check the sign of each factor across different intervals of t (for t greater than or equal to 0). On [0, 1), both (t - 1) and (t - 3) are negative, so their product is positive, meaning v(t) > 0: the object moves in the positive direction. At t = 1, v = 0: momentarily at rest. On (1, 3), (t - 1) is positive but (t - 3) is still negative, so the product is negative, meaning v(t) < 0: the object has reversed and moves in the negative direction. At t = 3, v = 0 again: momentarily at rest. On (3, infinity), both factors are positive, so v(t) > 0 once more: the object moves in the positive direction again. Altogether, this describes an object that moves forward, stops, reverses and moves backward, stops again, then moves forward for good, a full round trip completed by t = 3.

It's tempting to assume v(t) = 0 always signals a direction reversal, but that isn't guaranteed. Consider s(t) = t^3, so v(t) = 3t^2. Here v(0) = 0, but v(t) is greater than or equal to zero for every t, positive on both sides of t = 0, never negative. The object slows to a momentary pause at t = 0 but keeps moving the same direction throughout; there's no reversal at all. The lesson is that v(t) = 0 always means momentarily at rest, but you need to check the sign of v(t) on both sides of that instant to know whether direction actually changes.
